answer.sourceLine: This is scripture quoted exactly, which is rarer than it sounds. The sentence is 1 Thessalonians 5:18 in the King James Version ↗, and the wording matches the 1611 translation character for character — including the archaic two-word “every thing” and the colon before “for this is the will of God,” both of which modern quotation usually tidies away. As for the author, the majority of New Testament scholars hold this letter to be authentic ↗ — Paul’s own writing rather than one composed in his name, which is not something that can be said of every epistle bearing it.

source.excerpt: Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
trail: We read the verse in Wikisource’s text of the King James Version ↗ rather than a quotation site, and compared it word by word. It reads: “In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.” That is an exact match, two-word “every thing’ and all.

The spelling is the tell. Modern renderings and quote aggregators almost always print “In everything give thanks,” closing up the two words. The 1611 translators wrote them separately, so a quotation that keeps them apart is being taken from the translation rather than from someone else’s memory of it.

Wikipedia’s article on the letter ↗ reports that “the majority of New Testament scholars hold 1 Thessalonians to be authentic” and calls it the earliest extant Christian text, dated by most modern scholars to AD 49–51. That matters for the attribution: for several New Testament letters, “did Paul write this?” is a genuinely open question, and for this one the scholarly weight sits firmly on yes.
source.excerptNote: The verse is the third of three terse commands, and it reads differently with the other two attached: “Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks.” Quoted alone it sounds like a sentiment about gratitude; in place it is the last beat of a rhythm, and the “for this is the will of God” clause grounds all three.

author.bio: Paul the Apostle, born Saul of Tarsus, was a Jewish Pharisee who persecuted the earliest Christians before a conversion experience turned him into the movement’s most effective missionary. He founded congregations across the eastern Mediterranean and wrote them letters that became the oldest documents in the New Testament — earlier than the gospels, and the closest thing we have to a contemporary voice from the first Christian generation. Several of the letters bearing his name are of contested authorship; this one is not, and most New Testament scholars accept it as his.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Wikipedia calls 1 Thessalonians the earliest extant Christian text — earlier than any of the gospels — and these closing verses are Paul at his most compressed, firing off short instructions to a young congregation he had been forced to leave sooner than he wanted. The three commands run together: rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in everything.

The precise wording also carries the weight of the claim. Paul writes “in every thing give thanks,” not “for every thing” — thanks offered within any circumstance, not gratitude for the circumstance itself. It is a distinction the verse is often quoted past, and the difference between a demanding instruction and a glib one.
context.pull: In every thing, not for every thing — one preposition carrying the whole weight of the verse.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Wikisource text of the King James Version renders 1 Thessalonians 5:18 as "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." — an exact match for the quoted wording, including the two-word "every thing".
The Wikisource KJV text of 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 reads "Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you."

Wikipedia states "The majority of New Testament scholars hold 1 Thessalonians to be authentic", calls it "the earliest extant Christian text", and reports that a majority of modern scholars date it to AD 49–51.
The Wikisource KJV text of 1 Thessalonians 1:1 opens "Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus, unto the church of the Thessalonians" — confirming the two co-senders named with Paul.
Wikipedia records the King James Version as perpetually copyrighted in the United Kingdom and de facto public domain elsewhere.
